claims.text: Tempered martensitic steels will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as tempering temperature increases.
Low-temperature tempering promotes a ductile condition in martensitic steel.
An intermediate tempering-temperature range favors impurity segregation and embrittlement.
High-temperature tempering restores ductility in martensitic steel.
The proposed initial martensitic steel has a fine lath structure.
The as-quenched or minimally tempered initial condition has relatively high ductility.
Stepwise increases in tempering temperature can span low-temperature ductile, intermediate embrittled, and high-temperature restored-ductility regimes.
A controlled atmosphere avoids oxidation during the tempering experiments.
Phosphorus or antimony segregates to grain boundaries during tempering.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, grain-boundary impurity segregation reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes a drop in ductility.
At sufficiently high tempering temperatures, further diffusion mitigates impurity concentration gradients.
Mitigation of impurity concentration gradients at high temperature restores ductile deformation mechanisms.
Ductility will vary nonmonotonically with tempering temperature, with a sharp intermediate-temperature decrease followed by recovery.
The as-quenched or low-temperature-tempered baseline has good ductility without significant impurity segregation.
Temper embrittlement occurs only within a narrow intermediate tempering-temperature window.
The material remains ductile at temperatures below and above the intermediate temper-embrittlement window.
The proposed temper-embrittlement effect is absent in high-entropy alloy systems.
The temperature boundaries and magnitude of ductility loss depend on impurity concentration and alloy composition.
